newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Ferries set to face EU rules on passengers lists.
newsitem.headline: Ferries set to face EU rules on passengers lists.

text.p: Ferry operators offering services out of EU ports will have to register the names, gender and age bracket of passengers and crew on longer voyages if EU ministers reach a deal on new rules this Wednesday.
The moves are intended to help rescue services target their efforts in the event of a disaster, giving them the information they need to know whether people remain to be saved.

Lack of such data added to the confusion and anguish felt by victims' relatives after the 1994 sinking of the "Estonia" in the Baltic and the 1987 capsize of the "Herald of Free Enterprise" outside the Belgian port of Zeebrugge.

If adopted, the rules would oblige operators running international or domestic services from EU ports to count passengers and crew before departure for short journeys and to record names and so on for trips exceeding 20 miles (32 km).
The idea behind counting passengers as a minimum is to ensure vessels do not exceed capacity and to help rescuers.

Britain has raised questions about passenger registration, saying it is difficult to manage, does nothing to improve safety or the efficiency of searches and risks distorting competition between ferries and other transport modes.
The point on competition refers to the busy cross-Channel routes, where ferry operators face fierce competition from services through the Channel rail tunnel.

The European Commission, meanwhile, has said lists are essential for the identification of those people killed or injured in an accident and for the treatment of legal issues related to the insurance and inheritance rights of dependents.

One part of the draft, designed with Italy's Straits of Messina in mind, allows for passenger numbers to be established by adding the maximum capacity of the railway wagons and other vehicles carried instead of by counting heads.
The Dutch, who as EU presidency holders are chairing the two-day ministerial meeting from Tuesday, have suggested the rules come into effect from the start of 1999.
